Like $π$, it cannot be written exactly as a fraction or as a terminating decimal.

front_blocks.md: How is the graph of $y = \text{e}^{-x}$ related to $y = \text{e}^{x}$?

back_blocks.md: It is the reflection of $y = \text{e}^{x}$ in the $y$-axis.
The pair are in the form `y = \text{f} \left(x\right)` and `y = \text{f} \left(- x\right)`, which is what produces that reflection.

back_blocks.md: It is the **natural logarithm**, the logarithm to base $\text{e}$: $\mathrm{ln} x \equiv \mathrm{log}_{\text{e}} x$.
Everything that is true of logarithms in general is therefore true of $\mathrm{ln}$ as well.

front_blocks.md: $\mathrm{ln}$ is a number, in the way that $\text{e}$ and $π$ are.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
$\mathrm{ln}$ is a **function**, so it needs something to act on before it means anything at all.
$\mathrm{ln} 5$ is a number, but $\mathrm{ln}$ by itself is not, any more than $\mathrm{sin}$ by itself is.

front_blocks.md: What is the relationship between $\text{e}^{x}$ and $\mathrm{ln} x$?

back_blocks.md: They are **inverse functions**, so each one undoes the other.
That is why $\text{e}^{\mathrm{ln}x} = x$, and why applying one of them to both sides of an equation strips the other away.

front_blocks.md: An equation reads `\text{e}^{\text{f} \left(x\right)} = \text{g} \left(x\right)`. How do you get at `\text{f} \left(x\right)`?

back_blocks.md: Take $\mathrm{ln}$ of both sides, which leaves `\text{f} \left(x\right) = \ln \text{g} \left(x\right)`.
It works the other way round too: `\ln \text{f} \left(x\right) = \text{g} \left(x\right)` becomes `\text{f} \left(x\right) = \text{e}^{\text{g} \left(x\right)}`.

front_blocks.md: $\mathrm{ln} x$ has no value when $x$ is zero or negative.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
No power of $\text{e}$ produces zero or a negative number, so there is nothing for the logarithm to return.

front_blocks.md: If $y = \text{e}^{kx}$ then `\frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} = \_\_\_\_\_\_`, and if $y = \text{e}^{-kx}$ then `\frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} = \_\_\_\_\_\_`.

back_blocks.md: If $y = \text{e}^{kx}$ then $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = k \text{e}^{kx}$, and if $y = \text{e}^{-kx}$ then $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = - k \text{e}^{-kx}$.
The constant from the power comes down as a multiplier, and $y = \text{e}^{x}$ is simply the case $k = 1$.

cards.front_md: If $y = \text{e}^{kx}$ then `\frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} = \_\_\_\_\_\_`, and if $y = \text{e}^{-kx}$ then `\frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} = \_\_\_\_\_\_`.
cards.back_md:
If $y = \text{e}^{kx}$ then $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = k \text{e}^{kx}$, and if $y = \text{e}^{-kx}$ then $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = - k \text{e}^{-kx}$.

The constant from the power comes down as a multiplier, and $y = \text{e}^{x}$ is simply the case $k = 1$.

front_blocks.md: What stays the same when you differentiate $\text{e}^{kx}$?

back_blocks.md: The exponential part itself: $\text{e}^{kx}$ reappears in the derivative unchanged.
Only a constant multiplier is added in front, which is what makes exponential derivatives unusually simple.

The minus sign comes down with the $3$, so a decay curve has a negative gradient everywhere along it.

front_blocks.md: The gradient of $y = \text{e}^{x}$ is never zero.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
The gradient equals $\text{e}^{x}$, which is positive for every value of $x$.
So the curve is always increasing and has no stationary points at all.

front_blocks.md: How do you find the gradient of $y = \text{e}^{2x}$ at $x = 0$?

back_blocks.md: Differentiate to get $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 2 \text{e}^{2x}$, then substitute $x = 0$.
Since $\text{e}^{0} = 1$, the gradient there is $2$.
